CALPERS "GOLDEN HANDSHAKE" EARLY RETIREMENT INCENTIVE (GOVERNMENT CODE § 20903) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · City of Example Public Works Department

CALPERS 'GOLDEN HANDSHAKE' EARLY RETIREMENT INCENTIVE — INTRODUCTION
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as Maintenance Worker II, Public Works Department with City of Example Public Works Department, a local public agency that contracts with the California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS). This information sheet describes California Government Code section 20903 — a statute in the Public Employees' Retirement Law that lets a CalPERS contracting agency's governing body offer eligible local members up to two years of additional retirement service credit (a program commonly called a "golden handshake") when the agency determines that an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services makes doing so in the agency's best interests, and specific statutory conditions are met. If City of Example Public Works Department has adopted a contract amendment or resolution under this section, its stated effective date is: January 1, 2027. It is not a notice that City of Example Public Works Department has adopted, or intends to adopt, this program, is not a certification, resolution, or contract amendment under this section, and does not itself grant, calculate, or guarantee any amount of additional service credit for Jordan Lee or any other employee. Completing it does not establish that any of the statutory conditions described below currently exist at City of Example Public Works Department, or that City of Example Public Works Department is even a CalPERS contracting agency that has elected to be subject to this section.

THE STATUTORY TRIGGER: IMPENDING CURTAILMENT OR CHANGE IN SERVICE, AND THE AGENCY'S OWN "BEST INTERESTS" DETERMINATION
Government Code section 20903 opens by identifying who may use it and why: the section applies when the governing body of a CalPERS contracting agency itself determines that an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services makes offering additional retirement service credit to eligible local members in the agency's own best interests. The statute frames this as a threshold determination the agency's own governing body makes — not a right an individual employee can independently trigger — and, by its own terms, that determination only opens the door to eligibility: a local member becomes eligible for the additional service credit only if a further set of lettered conditions also exist, several of which are addressed in other clauses of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Notwithstanding any other provisions of this part, when the governing body of a contracting agency determines that because of an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing service, the best interests of the agency would be served, a local member shall be eligible to receive additional service credit if the following conditions exist:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903 (California Legislative Information text), the section's opening sentence stating the impending-curtailment/change-in-service trigger and the agency's best-interests determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the section's opening sentence, which states the trigger and cross-references the lettered conditions that follow; it does not itself determine whether a particular agency's own governing-body determination of "impending curtailment" or "change in the manner of performing service" would be upheld if challenged. No reported California appellate decision interpreting this specific statutory phrase was located: a CourtListener case-law search for the exact phrase "impending curtailment" together with "retirement service credit" returned zero results in this session. This clause also does not address whether a court would review such a determination at all, or under what standard, if an employee or taxpayer challenged it — a threshold and standard-of-review question this clause does not research.

CONDITION (A): THE RETIREMENT WINDOW THE AGENCY DESIGNATES MUST RUN BETWEEN 90 AND 180 DAYS
One of the section's lettered conditions ties eligibility to timing the agency itself sets. A member is eligible only if the member is employed in a job classification, department, or other organizational unit the agency's governing body has designated, and retires within a window the agency designates — either in the contract amendment that first adopts this section, or in a later resolution the governing body adopts for a subsequent round. The statute bounds how long that window may run: not less than 90 days, and not more than 180 days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The member is employed in a job classification, department, or other organizational unit designated by the governing body of the contracting agency and retires within any period designated in and subsequent to the effective date of the contract amendment, or any additional period or periods designated in any subsequently adopted resolution of the governing body of the contracting agency, provided the period is not less than 90 days nor more than 180 days."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(a) (California Legislative Information text), the designated job classification/unit and the 90-to-180-day retirement window condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (a) exactly; it does not itself state what window, if any, a specific contracting agency has designated, or when a window opens or closes for a specific employee — those facts depend on the agency's own contract amendment or subsequently adopted resolution, not on the statute's text alone. It also does not address how "job classification, department, or other organizational unit" is defined for a specific agency, a designation the statute leaves entirely to the agency's own governing body, and does not address what happens if an agency designates a window shorter than 90 days or longer than 180 days by mistake.

CONDITION (C): A 1 PERCENT LAYOFF CERTIFICATION MEASURED AGAINST THE AGENCY'S OWN DESIGNATED UNIT
The governing body may not simply decide, without more, that offering the credit serves the agency's best interests. It must also certify that it is electing to use this section because of impending mandatory transfers, demotions, and layoffs that meet a specific numeric threshold: at least 1 percent of the job classification, department, or organizational unit the governing board itself has designated, resulting from the curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, the agency's services.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The governing body shall certify that it is electing to exercise the provisions of this section, because of impending mandatory transfers, demotions, and layoffs that constitute at least 1 percent of the job classification, department, or organizational unit as designated by the governing board, resulting from the curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(c) (California Legislative Information text), the governing body's certification of impending transfers, demotions, and layoffs meeting a 1 percent threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (c) exactly. The statute measures "at least 1 percent" against "the job classification, department, or organizational unit as designated by the governing board" — a base the agency's own governing body defines for this purpose, not a fixed, agency-wide, or independently verifiable headcount. This clause does not calculate whether any specific number of transfers, demotions, or layoffs meets that 1 percent threshold at a particular agency, and does not address how, or whether, a governing body's designation of the relevant unit could itself be reviewed or challenged by an employee or member of the public.

CONDITION (D): A CERTIFIED INTENT TO LEAVE AT LEAST ONE RESULTING VACANCY PERMANENTLY UNFILLED
The section also requires the governing body to certify its own intent, made at the time the section is made operative, that the program will actually shrink the workforce rather than simply rotate who fills existing positions. Specifically, the governing body must certify that if any early retirements are granted after a member receives service credit under this section, any vacancies thus created — or at least one vacancy in any position in any department or other organizational unit — will remain permanently unfilled, resulting in an overall reduction in the workforce of the department or organizational unit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The governing body shall certify that it is its intention at the time that this section is made operative that if any early retirements are granted after receipt of service credit pursuant to this section, that any vacancies thus created or at least one vacancy in any position in any department or other organizational unit shall remain permanently unfilled thereby resulting in an overall reduction in the workforce of the department or organizational unit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(d) (California Legislative Information text), the certified intent that a resulting vacancy remain permanently unfilled (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (d) exactly. The statute requires only a governing-body certification of intent, made "at the time that this section is made operative," that a resulting vacancy — in any department or organizational unit, not necessarily the same one a particular retiring member left — will remain permanently unfilled; it does not require, and this clause does not address, any ongoing monitoring or enforcement mechanism confirming that an agency's later staffing decisions actually matched that certified intent, nor does it address what remedy, if any, would exist if an agency later filled a position it had certified would remain vacant.

CONDITION (E): A FLAT TWO YEARS OF ADDITIONAL SERVICE CREDIT, REGARDLESS OF A MEMBER'S ACTUAL YEARS SERVED
The headline benefit itself is a fixed, non-proportional amount: the statute sets the amount of additional service credit at two years, regardless of how much service credit the member already has. A member with only a few years of actual credited service and a member with decades of service both receive the same flat two-year addition under this subdivision, if the section's other conditions are met.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "The amount of additional service credit shall be two years regardless of credited service."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(e) (California Legislative Information text), the flat two-years-of-additional-service-credit rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (e) exactly; it states only the amount of service credit added (two years, regardless of credited service), not the dollar value that credit produces under a particular member's own retirement formula, final compensation, and age at retirement — a calculation this clause does not perform. A separate subdivision of the same section, subdivision (h) (not independently quoted in this document), narrows this benefit further for a member who is not currently employed by the contracting agency during the subdivision (a) window and who has less than five years of service credit; this clause does not analyze that additional condition in depth, and a reader should not assume the flat two-year credit applies without also checking subdivision (h) and the other lettered conditions addressed elsewhere in this document.

CONDITION (F): DISQUALIFICATION FOR RECEIVING UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PAYMENTS DURING THE WINDOW
The section builds in a specific disqualifying event tied to a different benefit system entirely. A member who would otherwise be eligible for the additional service credit is disqualified from this section if the member receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period — that is, during the retirement window the agency has designated under subdivision (a).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "This section is not applicable to any member otherwise eligible if the member receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(f) (California Legislative Information text), disqualification for receiving unemployment insurance payments during the specified period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (f) exactly. The statute disqualifies a member who "receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period" — it does not itself redefine "the specified period" here (that phrase refers back to the window period a governing body designates under subdivision (a), addressed in a separate clause of this document), does not address whether disqualification would also result from unemployment insurance payments received before the window opens or after it closes, and does not address how this rule interacts with the general California Unemployment Insurance Code eligibility and disqualification rules this project addresses in separate documents outside this one. This is a narrow, agency-side eligibility condition for the additional service credit, not a restatement of general unemployment insurance law.

CONDITION (G): FORFEITING THE ADDED CREDIT UPON SUBSEQUENT REENTRY INTO THE SYSTEM
The credit is not necessarily permanent once granted. The statute provides that any member who qualifies for the additional service credit under this section, upon subsequent reentry into the retirement system, forfeits the service credit that had been acquired under this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Any member who qualifies under this section, upon subsequent reentry to this system shall forfeit the service credit acquired under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(g) (California Legislative Information text), forfeiture of the added service credit upon subsequent reentry to the retirement system (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (g) exactly. The statute does not itself define what counts as "subsequent reentry to this system" — for example, whether reemployment in any position covered by the Public Employees' Retirement Law with any contracting agency counts as reentry, or only reemployment with the same agency that granted the credit — and does not state any time limit after which reentry would no longer trigger forfeiture. This clause does not research CalPERS' own regulations or administrative guidance interpreting "reentry" for this purpose, and does not address whether forfeiture affects only the two years of added credit or any other, separately earned service credit.

CONDITION (I): THE AGENCY MUST AFFIRMATIVELY ELECT INTO THIS SECTION THROUGH A PUBLIC, NON-CONSENT-CALENDAR PROCESS
A CalPERS contracting agency is not automatically subject to this section merely because it contracts with CalPERS. The statute states that the section does not apply to any contracting agency unless and until the agency elects to be subject to it — by amending its CalPERS contract in the manner prescribed for approval of contracts (without needing a vote among the employees), or, for contracts made after January 1, 2000, by express provision in the contract itself. Before a governing body may adopt this provision at all, the statute layers on a specific public process: with timely public notice, the governing body must place consideration of this section on the agenda of a public meeting, disclose the additional employer contributions and the funding for them, and give the public an opportunity to be heard — and the matter may not be placed on the agenda as a consent item. Only after that public meeting may the governing body adopt the section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "This section does not apply to any contracting agency unless and until the agency elects to be subject to the provision of this section by amendment to its contract made in the manner prescribed for approval of contracts, except an election among the employees is not required, or, in the case of contracts made after January 1, 2000, by express provision in the contract making the contracting agency subject to the provisions of this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(i) (California Legislative Information text), the agency's own election requirement to become subject to this section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  "Before adopting this provision, the governing body of a contracting agency shall, with timely public notice, place the consideration of this section on the agenda of a public meeting of the governing body, at which time disclosure shall be made of the additional employer contributions, and the funding therefor, and members of the public shall be given the opportunity to be heard. The matter may not be placed on the agenda as a consent item. Only after the public meeting may the governing body adopt this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(i) (California Legislative Information text), the public-meeting, non-consent-calendar prerequisite before adoption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=20903.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two consecutive parts of subdivision (i) exactly. It does not itself state whether any specific contracting agency has, in fact, elected to be subject to this section — that depends on the agency's own contract and contract amendments, which this clause does not look up for any specific reader. It also cross-references, but does not independently quote or analyze, Government Code section 7507 (a separate statute on actuarial cost disclosures the governing body must also comply with before adopting this section) and subdivision (j)'s savings clause for contracting agencies that had already adopted a now-repealed, earlier version of this same Section 20903 before its January 1, 1999 repeal — both are outside the scope of this clause.

THE TERM "GOLDEN HANDSHAKE" IN CALIFORNIA PRACTICE: A CAUTIONARY COMPARISON
The phrase "golden handshake" is not defined anywhere in the text of Government Code section 20903 itself; it is a colloquial label used in California public-sector practice for a temporary, agency-initiated early-retirement service-credit incentive of this general kind. In at least one reported California appellate decision, an employee's own contemporaneous letter — quoted by the Court of Appeal in reciting the case's undisputed facts — used the phrase "golden handshake" to describe a different institution's own, separate one-time early-retirement incentive program.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the special meeting will deal mainly with the ‘golden handshake’ early retirement scheme that the President contemplates to present to the Regents at their September meeting."
  — Bunnett v. Regents of University of California, 35 Cal. App. 4th 843 (1995) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2257037/bunnett-v-regents-of-university-of-california/)
  Known gap: This citation is offered only to document that California practice uses the term "golden handshake" for early-retirement service-credit incentives generally; it is not authority interpreting Government Code section 20903 itself. The quoted sentence is an employee's own letter, quoted by the Court of Appeal solely in its recitation of undisputed facts — not a statement of law, a holding, or the court's own characterization of the program. The "golden handshake" program actually at issue in this case was the University of California's own separate retirement plan (the University of California Retirement Plan and its "Plus 5" early-retirement addendum), which is not CalPERS, is not governed by the Public Employees' Retirement Law, and is not subject to Government Code section 20903; the case's actual holding — about contract interpretation and administrative-mandate review of the University's own denial of a different, unrelated retirement-incentive application — does not address, and this clause does not extend it to, any question about a CalPERS contracting agency's obligations under Section 20903. No reported California decision interpreting Government Code section 20903 by name, or squarely addressing a CalPERS local member's eligibility dispute under it, was located in this session's CourtListener searches (a search for "Section 20903" together with "PERS" and "additional service credit" returned zero results, and this session's CourtListener query quota limits how exhaustive that search could be).

SIGNATURE
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 8, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself determine that City of Example Public Works Department has elected to be subject to Section 20903, that any of the section's lettered conditions currently exist at City of Example Public Works Department, or that Jordan Lee is, or will be, eligible for any amount of additional retirement service credit. It is not a certification, resolution, contract amendment, CalPERS filing, or court filing, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, CalPERS' own published guidance, the contracting agency's specific contract with CalPERS, or a licensed attorney.]

citations.quote: Before adopting this provision, the governing body of a contracting agency shall, with timely public notice, place the consideration of this section on the agenda of a public meeting of the governing body, at which time disclosure shall be made of the additional employer contributions, and the funding therefor, and members of the public shall be given the opportunity to be heard. The matter may not be placed on the agenda as a consent item. Only after the public meeting may the governing body adopt this section.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes two consecutive parts of subdivision (i) exactly. It does not itself state whether any specific contracting agency has, in fact, elected to be subject to this section — that depends on the agency's own contract and contract amendments, which this clause does not look up for any specific reader. It also cross-references, but does not independently quote or analyze, Government Code section 7507 (a separate statute on actuarial cost disclosures the governing body must also comply with before adopting this section) and subdivision (j)'s savings clause for contracting agencies that had already adopted a now-repealed, earlier version of this same Section 20903 before its January 1, 1999 repeal — both are outside the scope of this clause.

expectedJSON.body: The phrase "golden handshake" is not defined anywhere in the text of Government Code section 20903 itself; it is a colloquial label used in California public-sector practice for a temporary, agency-initiated early-retirement service-credit incentive of this general kind. In at least one reported California appellate decision, an employee's own contemporaneous letter — quoted by the Court of Appeal in reciting the case's undisputed facts — used the phrase "golden handshake" to describe a different institution's own, separate one-time early-retirement incentive program.

citations.case: Bunnett v. Regents of University of California
citations.quote: the special meeting will deal mainly with the ‘golden handshake’ early retirement scheme that the President contemplates to present to the Regents at their September meeting.

expectedJSON.gap: This citation is offered only to document that California practice uses the term "golden handshake" for early-retirement service-credit incentives generally; it is not authority interpreting Government Code section 20903 itself. The quoted sentence is an employee's own letter, quoted by the Court of Appeal solely in its recitation of undisputed facts — not a statement of law, a holding, or the court's own characterization of the program. The "golden handshake" program actually at issue in this case was the University of California's own separate retirement plan (the University of California Retirement Plan and its "Plus 5" early-retirement addendum), which is not CalPERS, is not governed by the Public Employees' Retirement Law, and is not subject to Government Code section 20903; the case's actual holding — about contract interpretation and administrative-mandate review of the University's own denial of a different, unrelated retirement-incentive application — does not address, and this clause does not extend it to, any question about a CalPERS contracting agency's obligations under Section 20903. No reported California decision interpreting Government Code section 20903 by name, or squarely addressing a CalPERS local member's eligibility dispute under it, was located in this session's CourtListener searches (a search for "Section 20903" together with "PERS" and "additional service credit" returned zero results, and this session's CourtListener query quota limits how exhaustive that search could be).

I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 8, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California Government Code section 20903 — the Public Employees' Retirement Law's statutory basis for a CalPERS contracting agency's "golden handshake" program of up to two years of additional retirement service credit, including the section's impending-curtailment/change-in-service trigger, the 90-to-180-day retirement window condition, the 1 percent layoff-certification condition, the permanent-vacancy workforce-reduction condition, the flat two-years-of-credit rule, the unemployment-insurance disqualification rule, the reentry-forfeiture rule, and the agency's own election and public-meeting prerequisites to adopting the section — and a reported California decision's use of the colloquial term "golden handshake" in a different, non-CalPERS context. It does not itself determine that City of Example Public Works Department has elected to be subject to Section 20903, that any of the section's lettered conditions currently exist at City of Example Public Works Department, or that Jordan Lee is, or will be, eligible for any amount of additional retirement service credit. It is not a certification, resolution, contract amendment, CalPERS filing, or court filing, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, CalPERS' own published guidance, the contracting agency's specific contract with CalPERS, or a licensed attorney.]
